query_snapshot: According to NBS Circular 592, which molybdenum-bearing stainless-steel types were reported as most resistant to sulfuric acid at low temperatures, and what limitations prevent treating that statement as a universal material recommendation?
final_answer:
Evidence-grounded answer:

- NBS Circular 592 reports that molybdenum-bearing austenitic stainless steels Types 316 and 317 were most resistant to sulfuric acid at low temperatures. [nbscircular592.pdf, pp. 59-60, chunk b0a15485]
- The Circular states that resistance of stainless steels to sulfuric acid decreases with increasing temperature and that by about 150°F stainless steels corrode in many concentrations. [nbscircular592.pdf, pp. 59-60, chunk b0a15485]
- The Circular (citing Roach & Hall) reports Mo-bearing stainless steels were useful at room temperature only for certain sulfuric acid concentration ranges (e.g., below ~15% and above ~85% as noted in the Circular). [nbscircular592.pdf, pp. 59-60, chunk b0a15485]
- The Circular warns that corrosion performance may vary with corrodent concentration, impurities (including oxygen), temperature, alloy composition and prior history, surface condition, contact with dissimilar metals, and other service factors. [nbscircular592.pdf, pp. 59-60, chunk b0a15485]
- The Circular notes that additions of molybdenum reduce but do not eliminate susceptibility to localized attack (for example, pitting) and that specific environments (e.g., halide-containing solutions) can change alloy behavior. [nbscircular592.pdf, pp. 59-60, chunk b0a15485]
